title: The mountains sang with Dawud
hook: the mountains and birds echo Dawud's praise, and iron is made soft in his hand (34:10–11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: salawat, blessings that start with Allah and the angels, then reach the believers. Your line was blessings on him.

Stand in a stone stairwell, or under a highway bridge, and hum one low note. The walls hum it back. Children find this out on their own, and then they do it twice. Surah thirty-four, Saba', opens its stories with a man whose praise did that on a scale no stairwell could manage. He sang, and the hills answered. The birds joined in. And the same hands that held the song could bend iron like clay. His name is Dawud, the David of the Psalms.

Verse ten. Allah gave Dawud a grace, and then speaks to the landscape. Pickthall: "O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise!" The verb, awwibi, carries the sense of returning, again and again, the way an echo does. The hills don't just hear him; they give the praise back. Surah Sad says it too: the mountains glorified with him at nightfall and at sunrise, and the birds gathered. In the Qur'an, Dawud is given the Zabur, a scripture Muslims connect with the Psalms. A hadith shows how his voice was remembered. When the Prophet ﷺ heard his companion Abu Musa reciting beautifully, he told him he'd been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud. A voice like Dawud's became a way to praise a reciter. Then verse ten turns: and We made the iron supple for him. Verse eleven tells him to make coats of mail and to measure the links well. The singer is also a smith. Another hadith adds that Dawud ate only from the work of his own hands, though he was a king. The same man lifts praise so beautiful the mountains join, and sits at a workbench getting the rings of armor the right size. The verse ends with an instruction to him and his family: work righteousness. Worship and work, in one pair of hands.
screen: `A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAWUD.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, or want to try, quietly hum or say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, a few times, letting the sound fill your chest. If that isn't yours, hum one low note and feel where it lands, in your body, then in the room, as the room gives a little of it back. Then let the sound stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves.
Awwibi, the word telling the hills to echo Dawud's praise, again and again, like a returning echo, while the birds join in. Today's word.
Your line: the mountains sang along. Praise from a king who also measured rings. Tomorrow, his son, and a walking staff.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Dawud as a prophet given the Zabur; beautiful Qur'an recitation is still praised by comparing it to his voice, and many Muslims glorify Allah aloud or quietly with subhanallah throughout the day.

what a scholar hears: awwibi, from the root of returning (a-w-b), pictures the echo; Surah Sad 38:18–19 adds nightfall and sunrise, and Bukhari keeps the 'flute of the family of Dawud' hadith.

chat.says: Why does the Qur'an say the mountains praised along with Dawud?
options: Verse ten tells the hills and birds to echo his praise; they give it back.
It's a poetic way of saying Dawud mostly sang outdoors, in the hills.
Because Dawud could command mountains to do whatever he personally wished.
chat.meaning: In Saba' 34:10, Allah tells the hills and birds, awwibi: echo his praise. The word carries returning, again and again, like an echo.
